issues.printed: une K-algèbre A admet au plus une norme spectrale pour laquelle elle est complète
issues.correction: Retain a specified topology, or assume the identity between the two complete normed algebras is continuous in one direction. Then open mapping and the valid fixed-topology uniqueness argument apply. The maximum of two complete norms on the same algebra need not be complete.
issues.reason: Let C=C_p, F=Q_p-bar⊂C. Choose t in C outside F, extend t to a transcendence basis of C/F, and extend the automorphism t↦pt of its rational function field to σ∈Aut(C/F). Set ρ_1(x)=|x| and ρ_2(x)=|σ(x)|. Both are complete multiplicative Q_p-algebra norms, but ρ_2(t)=|p|ρ_1(t)≠ρ_1(t). Choose a_n∈F converging to t for ρ_1. Since σ fixes F, this sequence is Cauchy for max(ρ_1,ρ_2), while its individual limits are t and σ^(-1)(t)=p^(-1)t. Thus the maximum is not complete. The report gives all steps and the auxiliary field-theory inputs. This refutes the isolated stronger assertion and its proof step, not the main ramified theorem; an audit of all downstream uses remains open.

issues.correction: Replace the unique-choice definition by a solution-set/existence interface pending a repaired theorem with extra conditions. The two printed test conditions alone do not determine a vector for n=m=2. Also remove the assertion that all restricted Speh vectors lie in Pi.
issues.reason: For n=m=2, G'=GL2,V'=1,T'=id and all formal W^0 are left-N'-invariant. With u=[[1,varpi^-1],[0,1]], f=1_(uK')-1_K' is a nonzero right-K'-invariant compact function annihilated by every test integral by left translation (det u=1). Extend f to D=V iota(G') using Psi. Lapid–Mao20 Cor3.13/3.15 supplies a Shalika vector with this restriction; right averaging preserves f. Adding it to the L=1 essential vector gives a second solution. The proof's character claim fails explicitly: (I+tE13)(I+bE32)(I-tE13)=I+bE32+tbE12, so Psi changes by psi(tb). See report for full argument and limits.

issues.locator: Proposition 14, pp.725–727, and Remark 16, p.727, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 709–744 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 814976ee…f40a); also footnote 4, p.712
issues.printed: Proposition 14: close CM points of the same type with the same projection to X(1)×X(1) lie on a low-degree Hecke curve, stated for Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points alike. Remark 16: "Hecke curves do not pass through anti-Heegner CM points. Thus, …" anti-Heegner CM points repel. Footnote 4: the 2-to-1 ambiguity of [BT13] "can be rectified by using the stronger repulsion statement found in Proposition 14."
issues.correction: Proposition 14 holds for Heegner CM points (CM⁺) only, with Lemma 15 applied with h₀ = 1 (erratum Proposition 2.1). Close anti-Heegner CM points lie on low-degree conjugate Hecke curves instead. The first clause of Remark 16 (Hecke curves contain no anti-Heegner points) is true; its repulsion claim is false.
issues.reason: The real-analytic involution conjugating the second factor preserves the hyperbolic metric and swaps Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points, so anti-Heegner points cannot all repel. In general no h₀ ∈ SL₂(Z) reduces to the non-identity coset of the stabilizer H in its normalizer, which is where the proof fails (erratum §§1–2). The appeal in footnote 4 therefore rests on the withdrawn part; the main theorems hold by the corrected argument of the erratum.

issues.printed: Theorem A: "Let X be a smooth, proper and geometrically irreducible real variety, of dimension d ≥ 1. Assume that X satisfies the real integral Hodge conjecture for 1-cycles and that H²(X, O_X) = 0. … (ii) There exists a geometrically irreducible curve of even geometric genus in X if and only if the natural map Pic(X)[2^∞] → Pic(X_C)^G[2^∞] is onto." Theorem 3.16 assumes "dim(X) > 0".
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis d ≥ 2 (or X(R) = ∅); the proof, which goes through Proposition 3.9, needs d ≥ 2 when X(R) ≠ ∅.
issues.reason: Counterexample in dimension one: X = E, the real elliptic curve y² = x³ − x. Here H²(E, O_E) = 0 and the Hodge conjecture for 1-cycles (codimension 0) holds. The only geometrically irreducible curve in E is E itself, of geometric genus 1, so the left side fails. Since E(R) ≠ ∅, Br(R) → Br(E) is injective and Pic(E) → Pic(E_C)^G is an isomorphism, so the right side holds. Proposition 3.9 (a curve of odd geometric genus exists) is stated for dimension ≥ 2, as the introduction says (p.4). The surface and higher-dimensional cases, which are the paper's applications, are unaffected. Found by the extraction (items printed-even-genus, main-even-genus).

issues.locator: §4, the paragraph after Corollary 15 on parabolic curves, v3 p.11 (published p.141), in arXiv 2108.13397v3 (15 September 2023, the final author version; PDF SHA-256 e23989fb…b722); published page numbers are those the extraction recorded from the open-access publisher PDF (SHA-256 77c20bc7…e148), which could not be re-fetched here
issues.printed: "We say that a curve X is parabolic if it has genus 0 and the degree of X̄ ∖ X is at most 2. If X is proper of genus 0, then there is a unique Galois section, and it is geometric if and only if X = P¹. If X is parabolic affine, every Galois section of X is cuspidal (the only non-trivial case is settled by [Sch15, Theorem A]). Because of this, we can always assume that X is non-parabolic."
issues.correction: The sentence is false as stated. What the later reductions need is a statement about the t-birationally liftable (or birationally liftable) sections of a parabolic affine X, which have to be treated directly, including the case where X̄ ∖ X is a single point of degree 2. The reductions to non-parabolic X rest on this: "We may assume that X is non-parabolic" in the proof of Lemma 16, and "it is immediate to check that t-b.l. sections are quasi-t-b.l." after Definition 18, where the identity map is not available for parabolic X.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let k = Q and X = P¹_Q ∖ V(T² − 2). Then X is affine, of genus 0, with boundary a single point of degree 2, so it is parabolic. The paper defines a Galois section to be cuspidal if it is associated with a k-rational point of X̄ ∖ X (§1). The boundary has no Q-rational point, so X has no cuspidal sections. But 0 ∈ X(Q), so X has a geometric section. Schmidt's theorem concerns the existence of rational points and splitting; it does not make a degree-2 boundary point rational. The paper's Theorems A–C are not claimed to fail here, only this justification of the reduction. Noted by the extraction (item 77, with the reduction gap in items 81, 96 and 112).

issues.printed: "For every open subset U ⊂ X, denote by ι_U(s) the image of s in S_{U/k}, by hypothesis it is cuspidal. By [Sti12, Theorem 17 (2)], there exists a unique rational point x ∈ X̄(k) associated with ι_X(s) … For every open subset U ⊂ X, denote by P_{U,x} ⊂ S_{U/k} the packet of cuspidal sections associated with x. … Since ι_U(s) ∈ P_{U,x} for every U ⊂ X and s is the limit of the sections ι_U(s), we get that s is cuspidal associated with x too."

For those, ι_U(s) is cuspidal at x, and S_{k(X)/k} = lim_U S_{U/k} may be computed along this family, so the conclusion follows.
issues.reason: The hypothesis of the lemma is that every birationally liftable section is geometric or cuspidal. If x ∈ X, then for opens U containing x the section ι_U(s) is the geometric section at x, which is not in the cuspidal packet P_{U,x}. So "ι_U(s) ∈ P_{U,x} for every U ⊂ X" fails for those U, although the limit argument goes through on the cofinal subfamily. Noted by the extraction (item 127).

issues.locator: Lemma 5.2(ii), p.956, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), 943–966 (Caltech repository copy of the publisher PDF, SHA-256 77ff3290…790e)
issues.printed: "(ii) The number of supersingular points in X₀(N)(F_{p²}) that correspond to supersingular elliptic curves over F_{p²} with the Frobenius trace a_{p²} = 2p or −2p and the j-invariant different from 0 and 1728 is at least µ(⌊(p−1)/12⌋ − 3/2 + (−3/p) + ½(−1/p)). In particular, there is a supersingular point with a_{p²} = 2p or −2p in X₀(N)(F_{p²}) over X(1)(F_{p²})∖{0,1728} that is unramified for π if p ≡ 1 mod 12 or p ≥ 31."
issues.correction: The "in particular" follows for p ≡ 1 mod 12 and for p ≥ 31 with p ≠ 47. At p = 47 the displayed lower bound is 0 and gives nothing. The existence of an unramified supersingular point at p = 47 comes instead from Lemma 5.2(iii), since 47 ≡ 2 mod 3.
issues.reason: The conclusion needs the lower bound to exceed the number of ramification points, which (i) bounds by µ/6. At p = 47: ⌊46/12⌋ = 3, (−3/47) = −1 (47 ≡ 2 mod 3) and (−1/47) = −1 (47 ≡ 3 mod 4), so the bound is µ(3 − 3/2 − 1 − 1/2) = 0 < µ/6. A computation over all primes 31 ≤ p ≤ 400 finds 47 as the only failure, and beyond that the floor term dominates. The main theorem is unaffected: Lemma 5.2(iii) covers p = 47, and Rubin's own verification (Remark 2.3) covers small p. Found by the review REV-PAPER-BURUNGALE-KOBAYASHI-OTA-21.

issues.locator: Theorem 2.1 and footnote 3, p.4, in arXiv 2506.03465v2 (11 October 2025), the version read; the passage is the same in v1 (4 June 2025)
issues.printed: "Theorem 2.1. Let the notation be as above. Then we have ξ(h²_Q) = ξ((h¹/z)_Q), an equality of ideals in Z_p[[G_{p∞f}]]⊗Q." Footnote 3: "The formulation in Theorem 2.1 is then identical with the one in [11, §7.2]."
issues.correction: ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(h²_Q)·∏_{𝔩|f, 𝔩∤p} ξ(Z_p[[G_{p∞f}/D_𝔩]]_Q), D_𝔩 the decomposition group of 𝔩; equivalently ξ((h¹/z)_Q) = ξ(H²_Q) with H² = lim_{K'} H²(O_{K'}[1/pf], Z_p(1)), which is the module of Johnson-Leung–Kings §7.2. The printed equality holds when every prime factor of f lies above p, and after localizing at height-one primes on components ramified at every 𝔩|f with 𝔩∤p.
issues.reason: z is generated by the elliptic units of the single modulus p^n f (Kato §15.5), whose projection to a character χ carries ∏_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p}(1 − χ(𝔩)Frob_𝔩^{−1}) (Johnson-Leung–Kings Lemma 7.7); JLK accordingly pair it with H² over O_K[1/pf]. BT's h² is the class-group limit, which Kato (15.6.2) identifies at height one with H² over O_K[1/p]. By purity, 0 → H²(O[1/p]) → H²(O[1/pf]) → ⊕_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p} Z_p[[G/D_𝔩]] → 0, and since D_𝔩 has Z_p-rank one each term is torsion but not pseudo-null. On the trivial-character component 1 − Frob_𝔩^{−1} is a non-unit even after inverting p, so the printed equality fails whenever f has a prime factor not above p, and footnote 3's "identical" is false for h². The same imprecision is in Kato's quotation of Rubin (Astérisque 295, Theorem 15.2(2)); Rubin's elliptic units include all moduli g|f.

issues.printed: "Lemma 3.15. With the previous notation, we have Σ_{x∈D(k)} Σ_{j=1}^{r} #{y ∈ C̃_j(k^alg) : ν_j(y) = x} ≤ (q + 1)r + 2q^{1/2} · Σ_{j=1}^{r} g_g(C_j)."
issues.correction: The count of geometric branches over k-points needs an extra term for the non-rational branches through rational singular points. For a geometrically integral curve C with normalization of genus g and arithmetic genus p_a, one has Σ_{x∈C(k)} #ν^{−1}(x) ≤ #C̃(k) + 2 Σ_x δ_x ≤ q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g). The constant q + 4q^{1/2} + 3 in Theorem 9.1 and in Theorems 1.5, 1.7, 10.1 and Corollaries 1.11, 1.14, 1.15, obtained from Lemma 3.15 in (9.8), is not established by the v2 argument.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let D ⊂ P² over k = F_3 be the projective closure of y² = x²(x − 1). It is geometrically integral (r = 1) with normalization P¹, parametrized by x = t² + 1, y = t(t² + 1), so g_g = 0 and the right side is q + 1 = 4. D(F_3) consists of (0,0), (1,0), (2,1), (2,2) and the point at infinity. The origin is an ordinary node with tangent cone y² + x² = 0. Since −1 is not a square in F_3, its two branches t = ±i are defined only over F_9. The left side is therefore 2 + 4 = 6 > 4. The proof's flaw: Lemma 3.17 correctly relates the product of Z*_{D,k}(ζT) over ζ ∈ μ_d to the zeta functions of the C̃_j over k′. But the zeros and poles of Z*_{D,k} cannot be read off from that product. Here Z*_{D,k}(T) = (1 + T)/((1 − T)²(1 − qT)), and the extra factor (1 + T)/(1 − T) disappears under T ↦ −T. The bound with q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g) follows from Weil's bound for C̃ together with b_x ≤ δ_x + 1 ≤ 2δ_x at singular points, and it is attained in the example. The general reducible, weighted sum in (9.8) needs the analogous count, including intersections of Frobenius-conjugate components. Noted by the extraction (gap G1, items bad-branch-bound and global-sum-source), which checked the page image.
issues.known: Apparently corrected in the published version, which was not seen: Balakrishnan–Caro (arXiv 2501.03483v2, Theorem 2.1) quote the published Corollary 1.15 as #W_2(Q) ≤ #W_2(F_p) + 6·(p−1)/(p−2)·(p + 4p^{1/2} + 5), where v2 has p + 4√p + 3.

issues.printed: "Proposition 2.2. For a finite, flat map R → R′ of local rings, an open subscheme V ⊂ Spec R, and an affine, smooth R-group scheme G, if (1) Γ(Spec R, O) ≅ Γ(V, O) via pullback; and (2) every G-torsor is trivial over R; then the following pullback is injective: H¹_et(V, G) ↪ H¹_et(V_{R′}, G). (2.2.1)" Proof: "… every element of X(V) lifts to (Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}))(V), so, by [Gir71, III.3.2.2], the map H¹_et(V, G) → H¹_et(V, Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′})) (2.2.2) is injective."

For noncommutative G, supply the missing step: for every G-torsor P over V, the twisted map (^P Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}))(V) → (^P X)(V) must also be surjective.

When G is commutative this is injectivity, because the map is a group homomorphism. For a noncommutative G, H¹ is only a pointed set. The fibre through the class of a torsor P is the orbit set of (^P H)(V) acting on (^P X)(V), for the twists by P (Giraud III.3.2; cf. Serre, Galois Cohomology, I.5.5, Cor. 2). If P extends to R it is trivial by (2), so the problem is exactly the torsors on V that do not extend. Proposition 2.2 is used only in the proofs of Proposition 2.3 (G = Res_{R′/R}(T_{R′})/T) and Corollary 2.4 (G = T, an R-torus), where G is commutative, so the main theorems are unaffected. issues.correction: There are only finitely many k-isomorphism classes of nonsuperspecial K3 surfaces X over k admitting a polarization H of such a degree 2md with (i)–(iii). The polarized pairs themselves need not be finite in number.
issues.reason: On a fixed eligible (X, H) of degree 2m_0 d, the line bundles H^{⊗ℓ^j} have degree 2(ℓ^{2j} m_0)d. Then m = ℓ^{2j} m_0 satisfies (i) and (ii), and (iii) is unchanged. This gives infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic polarized pairs on one surface; the paper does not require polarizations to be primitive. The proof bounds NS(X_k̄) and then the surfaces. issues.printed: "The t-adic completion of R_U is R̂_U = k[x][[t]]; we have F_U = Frac(R̂_U) = k(x)((t))."
issues.correction: Frac(k[x][[t]]) is a proper subfield of k(x)((t)). The erratum says this but gives the witness Σ_{n≥1} t^n/x^n, which lies in Frac(k[x][[t]]). A valid witness is Σ_{n≥1} t^n/x^{n!}.
issues.reason: The erratum's series equals t/(x − t), since 1/(x − t) = Σ_{n≥0} t^n/x^{n+1} in k(x)((t)), and x − t ∈ k[x][[t]]; so it is not in the complement. A correct witness: for c = a/b with a, b ∈ k[x][[t]], remove the common power of t so that b_0 ≠ 0, and let m = ord_x(b_0). The recursion c_n = (a_n − Σ_{i≥1} b_i c_{n−i})/b_0 gives ord_x(c_n) ≥ −m(n + 1). Every element of Frac(k[x][[t]]) therefore has x-poles growing at most linearly in n, while Σ t^n/x^{n!} has poles of order n!. The paper's general arguments use F_U = Frac(R̂_U), not this identification. Noted by the extraction, which also found the flaw in the erratum's witness.

issues.printed: "Corollary 1.1.15. Let G be an arbitrary connected reductive group over Q_p with a Q_p-rational Levi subgroup M. Let μ: G_m → M be a minuscule cocharacter and [b_M] ∈ B(M)_b such that ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible. Then there exists w ∈ W(G, M) := N_G(M)/M such that ([b_M], {w·μ}) is M-admissible." Proof: "(1.1.13) implies that there exists w* ∈ W(G*, M*) such that ([b_{M*}], {w*·μ*}) is M*-admissible."
issues.correction: Replace N_G(M)/M by the absolute Weyl group W(G, T) of a maximal torus T ⊂ M with μ ∈ X_*(T), as in Proposition 1.1.13. Equivalently: some G(Q̄_p)-conjugate μ′ of μ factoring through T makes ([b_M], {μ′}) M-admissible.
issues.reason: The printed statement fails already for split G. Take G = GL_3, M = GL_1 × GL_2 (blocks of sizes 1 and 2), μ = (0,1,0) and b_M = diag(p,1,1), which is basic in M. Then ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible: its Newton point (1,0,0) equals the dominant μ̄, and both have κ_G = 1. But κ_M(b_M) = (1,0), while κ_M(μ) = (0,1). Since the blocks have different sizes, N_G(M) = M, so W(G, M) is trivial and no w in it helps. The permutation of the first two coordinates, in W(G, T) = S_3, does. The proof transports to the quasi-split inner form and applies Proposition 1.1.13. That proposition gives w* in the absolute Weyl group W(G*, T*), not in N_{G*}(M*)/M*, so the proof establishes the corrected statement. The only use is in the proof of Corollary 1.1.17, p.13, for G not necessarily quasi-split. It cites "Lemma 1.1.13" (the quasi-split Proposition 1.1.13) in the form w ∈ W(G, T). The corrected Corollary 1.1.15 is exactly what that step needs, so the later results stand. Checked on the page images. Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 2, items N29 and N32), which also verified the Weyl-group computation by machine.

issues.printed: "Let G′ = G × T, equipped with the symplectic representation V′ = V ⊕ V. Let X′ = X × {h_T}. Then we have (G′, X′) ↪ (G_{V′}, H_{V′}). … Restricting the action of I_{s′_0} to A_T induces a map of Q-groups I_{s′_0} → T, and we consider the composite I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab. By Corollary 2.1.9, I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} is surjective, so the map I_{s′_0} → G^ab factors through I_{s_0}, as this is true over Q_ℓ for any ℓ ≠ p."
issues.correction: Take G′ = G ×_{G^ab} T, the pairs (g, t) with the same image in G^ab. This lies in GSp(V ⊕ V, ψ ⊕ ψ), and X′ = X × {h_T} still maps into it because h^ab is constant on X. The kernel of G′ → G is T ∩ G^der, which dies in G^ab, so the composite I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab does factor through I_{s_0}. The rest of the proof then goes through.
issues.reason: Read literally, the construction fails at two points. First, G × T acting on V ⊕ V does not preserve ψ ⊕ ψ up to a scalar when the similitude factors of g and t differ, so it is not a subgroup of G_{V′}. Second, the claimed factorization fails. The CM automorphisms (1, t), t ∈ T, act trivially on A_{s_0} and by t on A_T, and they preserve the tensors cutting out G × T. So 1 × T lies in I_{s′_0}, and also in the kernel of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0}. But under I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab it maps onto G^ab, as T is a maximal torus of G. So the map does not factor through I_{s_0} unless G^ab = 1. The same happens over Q_ℓ, so the justification "as this is true over Q_ℓ" fails too. Surjectivity of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} alone cannot give a factorization. What is needed is that the kernel maps trivially, and the fibre product above provides this. Lemma 2.2.8 is used in the proof of Proposition 2.2.2 (p.28). Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 7, item T23) as a descent gate; the analysis and the fibre-product repair are given here.

The proof divides by 2 and 3, and the comparison with the coefficient-free Markoff equation z₁² + z₂² + z₃² = z₁z₂z₃ via x = z/3 needs 3 invertible. If the image of (w, u, v) lands in V_{k,m} × V_{n,r} and the image of Tv lands in W_{n,r}, and if v restricts to u, then there exists g ∈ G(C) such that (w, u, v) = L(w, g, r)." issues.correction: "v restricts to u" is not defined, and read as the zeroth-order condition used in the proof, namely that the value of v is u, the theorem is false. A first-order compatibility must be added: du equals the first-order part of v applied to dw, as holds for every L(w, g, r), or the full chain-rule compatibility of the jet v along w with the jets of u. The proof's last step must use it.
issues.reason:
Work locally on a modular curve (n = k = 1) with Γ torsion-free, near a point where q′ ≠ 0. Put w(t) = 2t, u(t) = q(t) and v(t) = J_r q(id_r(t)). Then:
- The m-jets of u are those of q ∘ (z ↦ z/2) ∘ w, so they lie in V_{k,m}.
- v lies in V_{n,r}, and Tv lies in W_{n,r}, since v moves along the leaf through the identity.
- The value of v at t is q(t) = u(t).
By Theorem 11.2, any g with u = q ∘ g ∘ w is z ↦ γ(z/2) with γ ∈ Γ. For such g, J_r(q ∘ g) at w(t) = 2t has first derivative q′(t)/2, while v has q′(t), so (w, u, v) ≠ L(w, g, r) for every g. In the proof, the leaf decomposition of v gives g(t) = τ_{−t}, the translation, with trivial leaf constant and n(t) = τ_{−t} ≠ id, although the zeroth-order condition holds. Every L(w, g, r) satisfies du = v_1 dw, which fails here (q′ ≠ 2q′). The same wording is in arXiv v3. The Ax–Schanuel theorems themselves are not claimed to fail. issues.locator: Theorem 4.19, function-field case, p.101 (with the definition of maximal variation, §1.6, p.16); the same statement is Theorem 4.19 in arXiv v4, p.100, in the author manuscript dated 21 August 2024 (126 pp., the journal's revision date; SHA-256 b36f4860…813e)
issues.printed: "Theorem 4.19. Let K be either a number field or a function field of one variable. Let S be a quasi-projective variety over K. Let π : X → S be a smooth relative curve over S of genus g > 1 with maximal variation. Let α be a line bundle on X of positive degree on fibers of π. Then the following morphisms satisfy the relative Bogomolov conjecture: (1) the S-morphism i_α^m : X^m_{/S} → J^m_{/S} for any m ≥ dim S + 1 …", where (§1.6) maximal variation means that the moduli morphism S → M_{g,R} is generically finite.
issues.correction: For a function field K of a curve over k, the hypothesis must be maximal variation of a model over k (equivalently, as the proof says, bigness of the relevant adelic line bundles over k rather than over K), which excludes isotrivial families. With that hypothesis, or for K a number field, the statement stands.
issues.reason: Counterexample to the function-field case: k algebraically closed of characteristic 0, K = k(t), S = Spec K, X = C₀ ×_k K for a smooth projective curve C₀/k of genus > 1, and α of degree 1. The moduli morphism Spec K → M_{g,K} is a point, hence generically finite, so X → S has maximal variation in the sense of §1.6. But every point of C₀(k) has canonical height 0 in the constant Jacobian, and these points are Zariski dense in X, so part (1) fails for m = 1 = dim S + 1; constant products give the same failure for the other parts. The proof itself notes that "we need the bigness of the adelic line bundles over k instead of over K", which a constant family does not have. The main uniform Bogomolov theorem excludes isotrivial families and is unaffected. Found by the extraction (items 185–189, 262–266).

issues.locator: §4.6.3, statement of the relative Bogomolov conjecture, p.100, in the author manuscript dated 21 August 2024 (126 pp., the journal's revision date; SHA-256 b36f4860…813e)
issues.printed: "Let k be either Z or a field. Let K be a global field over k. Namely, K is a number field if k = Z; K is a function field of one variable over k if k is a field. … Recall that the relative Bogomolov conjecture of [DGH2, Conj. 1.2] asserts that, if dim Y < g, then there is a constant ε > 0 such that Y(L, ε) = {y ∈ Y(K̄) : ĥ_L(ι(y)) ≤ ε} is not Zariski dense in Y."
issues.correction: Over function fields the statement needs the usual exclusion of the constant part (for instance, that A has trivial trace or that Y is not constant); [DGH2] formulates the conjecture over number fields.
issues.reason: For a constant abelian scheme A = A₀ ×_k S and a constant subvariety Y generating it with dim Y < g (for example a constant curve of genus > 1 in its Jacobian), the constant points have canonical height 0 and are Zariski dense, so the conjecture as stated fails for function fields. No result depends on the conjecture itself; its function-field instances in Theorem 4.19 are E1. Found by the extraction (item 182).

issues.locator: §1.6, definition of stable curves, p.16, in the author manuscript dated 21 August 2024 (126 pp., the journal's revision date; SHA-256 b36f4860…813e)
issues.printed: "The curve is called stable if it is semistable with arithmetic genus g > 1, and any rational irreducible component of C_k̄ intersects other irreducible components at three or more points."
issues.correction: Count special points on the normalization: every rational component must have at least three points of its normalization lying over nodes, counting both branches of a self-node (the Deligne–Mumford condition). Equivalently, a smooth rational component meets the other components in at least three points, and a rational component with a self-node meets them in at least one.
issues.reason: The printed condition ignores self-nodes. For example, a rational curve with one node attached at one point to a smooth genus-one curve is a stable curve of genus 2 in the usual sense, but its nodal rational component meets the other component in only one point. The paper uses stable reduction and the moduli of stable curves from the literature, so the intended (standard) notion is clear. Found by the extraction (item 1 and report §8).
